display_name: Khaleeji Arabic (Gulf — KSA / UAE / Kuwait / Qatar / Bahrain / Oman)

saudi.notes: Najdi (central) most associated with KSA marketing; Hijazi (west) softer; Eastern Province closer to Bahraini.

emirati.notes: Distinctive 'ch' sound for ك (chthir for كثير); heavy English code-switching in Dubai marketing.

kuwaiti.notes: Closer to Najdi; influential in Khaleeji pop culture and media.

qatari.notes: Conservative tone; closer to Saudi Najdi than Emirati.

bahraini.notes: Influenced by Persian and Indian loanwords historically.

omani.notes: Distinctive — closer to Yemeni in some features; less commonly used in pan-Khaleeji marketing.

casual_social.description: Default for Gulf B2C social — warm, slightly more formal than Egyptian casual.

professional_casual.description: LinkedIn KSA/UAE — heavy English code-switching is expected in Dubai/Riyadh tech.

corporate_formal.description: MSA-leaning Khaleeji — banking, government, royal-court communication.

grammar_quirks: Demonstratives 'هذا/هذي' kept closer to MSA than Egyptian ده/دي
First-person verb prefix 'أ' often replaced by 'ا' in writing (ابغى = أريد)
Negation 'ما' before verbs (ما اعرف = I don't know)
UAE: ك → ch sound (chthir for كثير)

code_switching_patterns.english_in_arabic: Heavy in Dubai, Riyadh tech, and Khaleeji Gen Z. UAE Emirati youth especially mix English freely. Common in fashion, tech, F&B marketing.
rules: Saudi government/religious brands should minimize English.
UAE consumer brands often go 50/50 Arabic-English.
When unsure, default to lighter code-switching for Saudi vs. heavier for UAE.

do_not_use: Egyptian markers (ده، دي، إزاي، أوي، علشان) — wrong dialect
Casual irony in Saudi corporate — feels disrespectful
Slang older than 3 years — Khaleeji slang cycles fast

saudi_najdi: Direct, slightly formal, traditional respect markers
emirati: Heavy English mix, cosmopolitan, fashion-forward tone
kuwaiti: Pop-culture influenced, expressive, slightly louder register
